extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy (readers of Kant)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kant's criteria for what counts as a moral law, duty, and morally valid maxim (focus on autonomy, heteronomy, universality, and the failure of empirical/material principles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of the will as sole principle of moral laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The autonomy of the will is the sole principle of all moral laws and of all duties which conform to them; the moral law expresses nothing else than the autonomy of the pure practical reason; that is, freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autonomy is self-legislation: the will must be determined by the mere universal legislative form of its maxim, independent of any material (desired object). Autonomy is the formal condition that makes a maxim fit the supreme practical law; it is freedom in the positive sense (self-legislation). Without autonomy maxims cannot be moral laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteronomy cannot ground obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Heteronomy of the elective will not only cannot be the basis of any obligation, but is, on the contrary, opposed to the principle thereof and to the morality of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the matter of volition (the object of a desire) enters into the practical law as its condition, the will is dependent on inclinations or physical law and does not 'give itself the law.' Such maxims lack the universally legislative form and therefore produce no obligation; they oppose pure practical reason even when resulting actions conform to the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: A practical precept with a material/empirical condition is not a practical law
rubrics_metrics.description: Hence a practical precept, which contains a material (and therefore empirical) condition, must never be reckoned a practical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws of a pure will bring the will into a non-empirical sphere; empirical (material) conditions yield only conditional universality (e.g., 'if I desire X, then do Y') and rest on private happiness. Such conditional rules cannot serve as necessary, universal practical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim must be capable of a universal legislative form
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of the elective will must be by the mere universal legislative form of which its maxim must be capable; only under this formal condition can maxims agree with the supreme practical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test a maxim, consider whether it could be willed as a universal law of nature. Example given: the maxim of telling untrue statements cannot be a universal law because statements would lose their force as proof. The form of universality, not the material end (e.g., one's own happiness), is what grounds obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of law may require restricting matter to achieve universality
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere form of law, which limits the matter, must also be a reason for adding this matter to the will, not for presupposing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: self-love as matter can be made objectively valid only if the maxim includes the happiness of others; this inclusion is required by the form of universality, not by a prior empirical motive. The form (universality) is the principle that determines the will and adapts inclinations to practical reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of private happiness (prudence) cannot found practical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of happiness may furnish maxims, but never such as would be competent to be laws of the will... it can supply only general rules, not universal; hence no practical laws can be founded on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness-based principles rest on empirical data and variable judgements. They give rules that often work but lack necessary universality. Distinction emphasized: 'The maxim of self-love (prudence) only advises; the law of morality commands.' Therefore prudence cannot substitute for categorical obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law must be simple enough for common understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law commands the most punctual obedience from everyone; it must, therefore, not be so difficult to judge what it requires to be done, that the commonest unpractised understanding... should fail to apply it rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral requirements should be such that even the commonest intelligence can, without worldly prudence, see what autonomy-based duty requires. By contrast, heteronomous (prudential) rules often require much prudence and worldly knowledge to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment must be justifiable as punishment (justice), distinct from happiness-consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In every punishment, as such, there must first be justice, and this constitutes the essence of the notion. Punishment is a physical evil... ought to be connected with moral legislation as consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment cannot be defined merely by the harm it brings to private happiness. Even if punishment is used benevolently to promote future happiness, it must first be justified as deserved harm. Treating punishment solely as means to happiness would undermine the concept of crime and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral feeling (satisfaction/dissatisfaction) cannot be the basis of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of morality and duty must... have preceded any regard to this satisfaction, and cannot be derived from it. A man must first appreciate the importance of duty to feel moral satisfaction or remorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories that reduce morality to a special moral sense or to feelings mistake effect for ground: one must have the concept of duty a priori; feelings may follow from practiced conformity but cannot found obligation. Anti-pattern: deriving moral law from sensations of pleasure/pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material/practical principles exhaustively listed are inadequate; only the formal practical principle suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Material Principles of Determination taken as the Foundation of Morality (subjective/objective × external/internal: education, civil constitution, physical feeling (Epicurus), moral feeling (Hutcheson), perfection (Wolf, Stoics), will of God (Crusius)) — those in the upper table are empirical and incapable of furnishing the universal principle of morality; the formal practical principle of pure reason is the only one possible to furnish categorical imperatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant classifies all candidate material principles (education, physical feeling, moral feeling, perfection, will of God, etc.) and argues they are either empirical or dependent on ends and so cannot yield necessary, universal moral law. The only adequate ground is the formal condition: the form of universal legislation of maxims (autonomy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction: moral law provides practical reality and evidence for freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law proves not merely the possibility of freedom, but that it really belongs to beings who recognize this law as binding on themselves; the moral law is a law of the causality of free agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because speculative reason could only posit freedom negatively, the moral law gives positive, practical reality to the concept of freedom by showing that reason can be an immediate determining principle of the will. This is offered as a kind of 'credential' for the moral law's objective validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law is given a priori and is apodictically certain
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral law is given as a fact of pure reason of which we are a priori conscious, and which is apodeictically certain, though for experience no exact fulfilment can be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective reality of moral law cannot be proved empirically; it subsists independently of empirical principles. Critique of practical reason begins with pure practical laws and their reality; the moral law is known by reason itself rather than by sensory intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: test a maxim by imagining it as a universal law of nature (universalizability test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the maxim which I am disposed to follow... is tested by the practical reason, I always consider what it would be if it were to hold as a universal law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete testing examples: (1) a maxim allowing untrue statements cannot be a universal law because it would destroy the force of testimony; (2) a maxim endorsing arbitrary suicide cannot be legislated in a system that maintains itself. This is the operational procedure for assessing maxims' fitness as laws.
